lead: A three-phase controlled rectifier takes three AC supplies spaced 120° apart and replaces diodes with thyristors. The phases share the load, so the DC output has less ripple and the supply currents are more balanced than in a single-phase circuit. Delaying each gate pulse by the firing angle α sets the average DC voltage. The output ripple repeats p times per supply cycle, where p is the pulse number. Such converters feed DC motor drives, battery chargers, electrolysers and high-voltage DC terminals.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for firing-angle control, and three-phase phasors for line and phase values.

blocks.text: Let the phase voltages be v<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> sin θ, v<sub>b</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> sin(θ − 120°) and v<sub>c</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> sin(θ + 120°). V<sub>m</sub> is the phase peak in volts. If V<sub>ph</sub> is the phase RMS voltage, V<sub>m</sub> = √2 V<sub>ph</sub>. The line RMS voltage is V<sub>L</sub> = √3 V<sub>ph</sub>.

A converter with p output pulses per supply cycle has its lowest ripple at p f, where f is the supply frequency in Hz. A single-phase full-wave rectifier has p = 2. The three-pulse half-wave circuit has p = 3. The six-pulse bridge has p = 6. Higher p gives smaller ripple and a smaller filter for the same load.
p = pulses per supply cycle; f<sub>ripple</sub> = p f
blocks.where: p is 3 for the three-pulse circuit and 6 for the six-pulse bridge; f is the supply frequency in Hz; f<sub>ripple</sub> is the lowest ripple frequency in Hz.

blocks.text: The three-pulse, or M3, circuit is a half-wave connection: one thyristor per phase, all cathodes joined, and the load returned to the neutral. Each device conducts for 120°. The six-pulse, or B6, bridge uses six thyristors, two per phase leg, and needs no neutral. Each device conducts for 120°, and a new conducting pair forms every 60°. That gives p = 6 and ripple at 6f.
Assume the DC current is continuous: the load inductor is large enough that i<sub>d</sub> never falls to zero. At any instant one upper and one lower thyristor conduct.

The firing angle α is measured from the natural commutation instant of each device: the angle where that device's anode voltage first becomes more positive than the cathode it works against, so the device becomes forward biased. With v<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> sin θ, v<sub>a</sub> equals v<sub>c</sub> at θ = 30°, so T1 is forward biased from θ = 30° onward; at α = 0 it conducts from 30° to 150°, with T6 already on. Firing T1 at θ = 30° + α starts conduction with T6. T2 joins 60° later, and so on. Each thyristor stays on for 120°. The bridge needs no neutral because the return path is through the conducting thyristor in the other leg, not through a neutral wire.
V<sub>dc</sub> = (3√3 V<sub>m</sub>/π) cos α = 1.35 V<sub>L</sub> cos α = 2.34 V<sub>ph</sub> cos α
blocks.where: V<sub>dc</sub> is the average DC voltage in V for continuous current; V<sub>m</sub> is phase peak in V; V<sub>L</sub> is line RMS in V; V<sub>ph</sub> is phase RMS in V; α is the firing angle in degrees, counted from the natural commutation instant of the device (θ = 30° for T1 with v<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> sin θ), not from the zero crossing of v<sub>a</sub>. The 1.35 already contains √3 and √2.

blocks.text: At α = 0°, Vdc ≈ 1.35 VL. At α = 90°, Vdc = 0. For α above 90°, Vdc is negative if current stays continuous and the load can supply energy; the bridge then works as an inverter. With a plain R load, current may become discontinuous at large α, and the formula overstates Vdc. A large RL load keeps current continuous. With an RLE load, current starts when the conducting pair's line-to-line supply voltage exceeds E (ignoring device drops); the averages then obey Vdc = E + IdR. See Chapter 2.6 for overlap.

The M3 circuit has three thyristors, one per phase, with cathodes common and the load between the common cathode and neutral. Each thyristor conducts for 120°. Current returns through the neutral, so the supply transformer secondary needs a neutral. Its average voltage for continuous current is V<sub>dc</sub> = 1.17 V<sub>ph</sub> cos α, where V<sub>ph</sub> is phase RMS in V.

A transformer may be delta-star or star-star. It isolates the converter, sets VL, and for M3 provides the neutral. The B6 bridge is standard for industrial DC drives because its 6f ripple is easier to filter and its supply current has less low-order harmonic content than the M3 circuit. The M3 circuit suits low-cost supplies where a neutral is available. Harmonic and power-factor measures are in Chapter 2.5.

figure.caption: The bars are plotted against θ, the angle in v<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> sin θ. T1 first becomes forward biased at θ = 30°, where v<sub>a</sub> = v<sub>c</sub>, so at α = 0 its bar runs from 30° to 150°. T6 starts at 330° and continues past 360° into the next cycle. Each thyristor conducts for 120° and a new pair takes over every 60°, so the output ripple is six times the supply frequency.

spec.aria: Six horizontal bars offset by 60 degrees, each 120 degrees long, starting at 30 degrees and ending at 450 degrees, showing when each thyristor of a six-pulse bridge conducts at a firing angle of zero.

examples.question: A three-phase fully controlled bridge is supplied from a 400 V, 50 Hz line. The DC current is continuous and the firing angle is α = 30°. (a) Find the average DC output voltage. (b) Find the lowest ripple frequency. (c) Compare with a three-pulse half-wave circuit using the same supply and α. Take cos 30° = 0.866.
steps: For the six-pulse bridge use V<sub>L</sub> = 400 V line RMS and α = 30°, so cos α = 0.866.
The pulse number is p = 6, so f<sub>ripple</sub> = 6 × 50 Hz = 300 Hz.
For the three-pulse circuit, V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>/√3 = 400 V / 1.732 = 230.94 V.
examples.answer: The bridge gives 467.6 V DC with 300 Hz ripple; the three-pulse circuit gives about 234.0 V at the same firing angle.
examples.check:
import math
cos30 = 0.866
vdc6 = 1.35 * 400 * cos30
frip = 6 * 50
vph = 400 / math.sqrt(3)
vdc3 = 1.17 * vph * cos30
print(round(vdc6, 1))
print(float(frip))
print(round(vdc3, 1))

traps: Using line RMS V<sub>L</sub> in V<sub>dc</sub> = 1.17 V<sub>ph</sub> cos α, or phase RMS V<sub>ph</sub> in V<sub>dc</sub> = 1.35 V<sub>L</sub> cos α. The 1.35 form wants line RMS; the 1.17 form wants phase RMS.
Multiplying 1.35 V<sub>L</sub> by √2 or √3 again. The factor 1.35 already includes both √3 and √2.
Saying each thyristor in a B6 bridge conducts 60°. Each conducts 120°; a new conducting pair appears every 60°.
Expecting a neutral connection for a B6 bridge. The three-pulse M3 circuit needs a neutral; the bridge does not.
Assuming V<sub>dc</sub> is always negative for α > 90°. The continuous-current formula and a load able to supply energy are both required.

quiz.q: What is the pulse number of a rectifier, and what is it for the M3 and B6 circuits?
quiz.a: The pulse number p is the number of output voltage pulses per supply cycle. p = 3 for M3 and p = 6 for B6.

quiz.q: Why does a six-pulse bridge need a smaller output filter than a three-pulse circuit?
quiz.a: Its ripple is at 6f instead of 3f and has lower amplitude, so a smaller inductor or capacitor removes it.

quiz.q: A B6 bridge runs from a 415 V, 50 Hz line with continuous current at α = 45°. Find V<sub>dc</sub> and ripple frequency. Use cos 45° = 0.707.
Explain how a B6 bridge can deliver negative average voltage while the current direction stays the same.
quiz.a: For α > 90° with continuous current, the average voltage reverses but the thyristors still carry current in the same direction. The load must supply energy; power flows from DC to AC, so the bridge acts as an inverter.

quiz.q: State the conduction angle of each thyristor and the interval between new conducting pairs in a B6 bridge.
quiz.a: Each thyristor conducts 120°; a new pair forms every 60°.

quiz.q: An M3 circuit has V<sub>ph</sub> = 230 V and α = 60°. Continuous current. Find V<sub>dc</sub>.
Why does the continuous-current formula overpredict V<sub>dc</sub> for a light R load at large α?
quiz.a: The load current falls to zero before the next thyristor is fired. The output then follows part of the supply voltage (line-to-line in the B6 bridge, phase voltage in the M3 circuit) instead of a continuous conducting pattern, so the average is lower than 1.35 V<sub>L</sub> cos α or 1.17 V<sub>ph</sub> cos α predicts.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, six-pulse bridges are basic building blocks in DC motor drives, electrolysis rectifiers and HVDC links; twelve-pulse and higher pulse arrangements combine bridges through phase-shifting transformers to cancel harmonics. Modern grid-connected converters often use voltage-source inverters with PWM instead, but controlled rectifiers remain in high-power DC supplies. Research directions include hybrid bridges, active front ends and fault-tolerant rectifiers. Search terms: six-pulse controlled rectifier, HVDC converter bridge, twelve-pulse rectifier, active front end.
